intro: The second violin hammers on D while the viola plucks like a drum: Bartók’s Second Quartet turns four string players into a fierce little dance band. The Carmel Quartet plays the fast central movement.

sections.label: A · Repeated D, plucked viola
sections.mNote: Second violin repeats octaves beneath a tightly turning melody

sections.label: B · Narrow tunes, repeated notes
sections.mNote: Quick repeated rhythms keep returning between the short tunes

sections.label: C · The dance leaves room for song
sections.mNote: The middle episodes include a high violin and plucked cello

sections.label: A′ · The repeated-note dance returns
sections.mNote: The four strings recover the insistent dance rhythms

sections.label: Coda · Prestissimo, with mutes
sections.mNote: The fastest passage begins pianissimo, with all four instruments muted

cues.title: D, over and over
cues.text: After a short introduction, the second violin repeats D in octaves while the viola plucks short notes. The melody curls above and below them, decorated with quick ornaments. The accompaniment has the persistence of a drum.
cues.evidence: Roger Parker, Gresham College lecture, 4 December 2007, describes the opening tritones, repeated second-violin D octaves, viola pizzicato and ornamented melody: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The road to Biskra
cues.text: In 1913 Bartók records Arab music around Biskra in Algeria. Its repeated rhythms and richly ornamented tunes feed this movement: the melodies turn within a small compass while the accompaniment hammers away.
cues.evidence: The 1913 recordings near Biskra are documented by Vera Lampert in Folk Music in Bartók’s Compositions: https://bartok-nepzene.zti.hu/en/introduction/ . Parker discusses the North African connection and the movement’s narrow melodies: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

cues.title: A violin above plucked cello
cues.text: The middle episodes make room for a high violin melody above plucked cello. Longer phrases interrupt the repeated-note dance; the singing line hangs well above the little plucked accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Parker describes the lyrical middle episode for high violin and pizzicato cello within the movement’s loose rondo form. This note covers the central group of episodes: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The quartet’s first players
cues.text: In Budapest on 3 March 1918, the Waldbauer–Kerpely Quartet gives the first performance. Bartók dedicates the score to the same four musicians: Waldbauer, Temesváry, Kornstein and Kerpely.
cues.evidence: Budapest Bartók Archives, chronological catalogue, BB 75: première date, ensemble and dedication: https://zti.hu/en/ba/bartok-compositions/chronology

cues.title: The dance grips again
cues.text: The repeated rhythms return, crowding the four string parts together. Short, ornamented tunes turn against the persistent accompaniment. The lyrical breathing space is over.
cues.evidence: Parker describes the movement’s recurring repeated-note dance and contrasting lyrical episodes: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2. The note uses the established return section.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Faster, with mutes
cues.text: The final Prestissimo begins pianissimo, with mutes on all four instruments. Bartók asks for a scarcely credible speed: 200 dotted minims a minute. The dance rushes past in a whisper.
cues.evidence: Parker discusses the score’s closing Prestissimo, its mute and pianissimo instructions and the metronome marking of dotted minim = 200: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A high violin above plucked cello
transitions.to: C · The dance leaves room for song
transitions.how: The central episodes interrupt the repeated-note dance with longer phrases. A high violin melody unfolds above plucked cello; the other string parts leave more room around it. The pizzicato keeps a small, dry pulse beneath the singing line.
transitions.evidence: Parker describes the lyrical middle episode for high violin and pizzicato cello. The section covers several central episodes: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

transitions.title: The repeated rhythms return
transitions.from: C · The dance leaves room for song
transitions.how: Short repeated notes restore the dance after the more lyrical episodes. The narrow, ornamented melodies again meet an insistent string accompaniment. The quartet trades its long phrases for the opening’s quick bow strokes and sharp accents.
transitions.evidence: Parker describes the returning dance rhythms within the movement’s loose rondo form: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2. The established section marks this return.

transitions.title: Mutes on for the Prestissimo
transitions.how: All four players put on mutes for the closing Prestissimo. Bartók asks for pianissimo as the speed increases, keeping the repeated notes and turning figures light. The metronome marking is dotted minim = 200.
transitions.evidence: Parker describes the final Prestissimo, played pianissimo with mutes, and its metronome marking: https://www.gresham.ac.uk/watch-now/bartok-quartet-no-2

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: He heard a future for concert music in village songs, and went out with a phonograph to learn how they were sung.
facts: István Thomán, a Liszt pupil, and Hans Koessler; Budapest Academy, 1899–1903
Piano professor in Budapest, 1907–34; folk-music research in Budapest and at Columbia University
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages; Biskra, 1913; Turkey with Adnan Saygun, 1936
Six quartets, three piano concertos, two violin concertos, three stage works and Mikrokosmos
composer.background:
In 1904 Bartók heard Lidi Dósa, a young woman from Transylvania, singing to the children in her care. He wrote down her songs. Here was Hungarian music unlike the urban entertainment that usually went by that name, and he wanted more of it. Two years later, collecting with Bartók, the writer Béla Balázs found that the frail-looking pianist could wear him out: “I was already very tired, but he kept urging and driving me on to collect more!” Balázs put the encounter in his diary.

Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós in 1881, when the town belonged to Hungary; it is now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. His father, director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven. His mother Paula supported Béla and his sister by teaching, moving between towns before settling in Pozsony, now Bratislava. At the Budapest Academy he studied piano with István Thomán, who had studied with Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler.
